en: Braced himself like a leopard.
Inspiration came to him from the unseen;
His bloodlust seized him fiercely,
He ground his teeth with a crack,
Gripped by valor, his fury boiling;
His thirst for blood possessed him.
When this gray wolf blazed with rage,
She gave you tea when you thirsted,
Listened freely to your words,
Cosseted you,
Hung necklaces around your neck,
Draped brocade over your back,
And, lest the sun’s heat touch you,
Had you tended in a shady place,
Entrusted you to attendants,
And had the chief wife praise you.
Did she not regard you as a nephew
And graciously listen to your words?
She listened to your fitting words as a daughter-in-law,
And regarded you as her own mother.
Yet you let your tongue run wild,
Incited your Kanchoro,
And destroyed your bloodthirsty lord.
You steeped your churn in poison,
And thus brought about your own end!
You placed sixty treasuries of jewelers
In Kanchoro’s hands;
You made Kanchoro destroy
The sixty Kalmyks, Bölökbay,
And Davut, master of the treasury.
You imposed punishment upon me
And had strips of hide cut from my back;
Into the palace where no cold-hearted man might enter,
You admitted Kanchoro.
You shook the Kyrgyz and made them your subjects,
And made heroes of whomever you chose.
Woman, if you understand, it was you
Who caused this monstrous revolt and great conflict.
You are an infuriated infidel,
An evil, witch-like infidel!
You utterly ended my laughter,
And scattered all my possessions;
You made my words mere meadow grass
And devastated my people.
Incorrigible shrew, you will never prosper;
Though you came here a wanderer, you bluster
And will not curb your pride.
May you and your husband be as one!
How you have enraged me,
And driven my spirit into grief;
Calling me a degenerate son of China,
You showed me filth to the very end.
My anger rises and I bristle;
Today I will surely fall upon one of you!
We were kin, yet you would not act as kin;
Regarding me as an enemy,
You had your troops close around me.
Pouring out your wrath and roaring,
You wicked woman remained incorrigible.
My fury has risen—you will die;
Today, accursed woman, you will see
The true place whence none return!
When I rise in wrath,
You will surely die today.
I have looked you full in the face,
Restless, vicious shrew;
Why have you provoked my anger?
Whom did I command to yield the throne?
Shall I strike away completely
That groundless rage of yours?
I called you kin, but you will not be kin;
You rage and will not mend your ways,
Forever hurling words at me.
When I regard you as my mother,
Why do you seek a quarrel?
From time to time,
You always begin yapping.
You make me shoot at you as an enemy
And plunge me into torment.
You roar and work yourself into a frenzy,
You shriek and speak outrageously.
You are an enemy openly revealed,
The black eye at the heart of conflict,
A clamoring, shrieking menace,
A shameless creature with tireless jaws.
When my heroic brother indulged me,
He gave me butter when I hungered,
It is also true that I am his son.
It is also true that I am the fierce one
Who overturned peoples and founded a realm.
It is also true that I was the mountain refuge
Of rolling Talas and great Chatkal.
It is also true that I am the lion
Who strips the life from any he meets.
Did I not pound the valley into dust?
When caught in a blood feud,
I laid even my own father in the grave;
When spears were leveled straight at me,
When one like you inflamed and scorched my soul,
I warred even against my kin.
I am conflict itself,
The black eye of rebellion!
To kin I am a golden banner,
To foes the roar of battle!
When anger makes me bristle,
I am fury itself;
I too am the black eye of conflict!
I ravaged his pastures and rendered them fat;
Hero Kyyaz, whom you desired—
I cut off his head and laid him low.
Bristling in my rage,
In the Seven Valleys I seized
The migration lands of the Jediger,
And took my revenge.
I extinguished the fire they had kindled
And drove them all away;
I felled their banner and raised an uproar,
And took Kyyaz Khan himself.
Slaughtering his people without sparing one,
I struck terror into their beys
And took my revenge by hemming them in.
When one comes to you calling you kin,
You twist his neck like an enemy;
Whenever I come, you shriek
And turn to bite my calf.
You grow ever more insolent;
May you and your husband be as one!”
As though you would rule everyone,
As though you would swallow the whole world,
You bristle when angered,
As though you would slaughter them all.
Your face blackens and darkens,
You cluck and rant in frenzy,
And still you stand there ranting.
Has your honored father Shaatemir—
Has your father Shaatemir died?
Have the people wailed and the nation cried out?
Has someone buried your father?!
When your slave comes pleading, calling you kin
And bearing no grudge,
You rage and threaten;
When your servant comes, you change your face
And rave as though your mother’s kin
Had all been massacred.
Before, you spoiled my temper;
You roused in me a rage no cudgel could quell.
Without cause you spoiled my temper,
Tormented every spoonful of my blood,
And made my whole soul boil!
Why did you come shouting and raging
To speak such cutting words?
Has some great slaughter befallen you?
Why did you provoke my wrath?
You are only a woman, yet you worked yourself up;
Had I left you to your own devices,
You raged as though you would devour me.
You shouted in anger,
And before even your husband, woman,
You summoned your executioners.
You fouled your tongue and made it a sheath,
Raised a clamor and started strife,
Calling me a fugitive son of the khagan,
A flesh-born slave of the bloodthirsty one;
You drive my blood from its course,
Shrieking your ceaseless abuse,
And thus bring about my end.
Of the fugitive who came from the khagan’s realm—
He thrust his hand inside her,
And the black blood of her heart
He scooped up in both hands and swallowed:
“Now my vengeance is sated;
Now what died in me has revived,
And my extinguished fire is kindled!”
While Külchoro was doing this,
Before Kanchoro could prepare against him,
Before Kanchoro could summon his courage,
Before he could unleash his fierce wrath,
Before his executioners could rush like wind
And reach him and surround him,
Before the people cried out and the nation panicked,
Before they could offer him as a sacrifice,
Before anyone could utter a word,
In the blink of an eye,
Aichürök, daughter of Akun,
Ready to die if death had come,
To stand as protector of Külchoro,
Her mighty mountain of support—
The wretched fairy-like beauty
Was torn by many thoughts;
Tears poured from her eyes,
Her heart boiled like embers.
Having donned black for the conflict,
How could she stand still?
Her wrist-thick hair came loose,
And tears flowing from both eyes
Streamed below her two breasts.
If conflict suddenly erupted,
If fate decreed his death,
How could she endure the loss
Of the brother-in-law who protected her?
His malice was deep, his venom strong,
A bloodstained destroyer of peoples,
That resourceful kinsman Kanchoro,
Yet his stature was that of a hero.
If the poor eagle were attacked,
If my brother-in-law were suddenly caught
In bitter, calamitous strife—
While she thought thus, Külchoro
Was seized by towering rage.
At the shrew upon the throne
He charged and swiftly reached her.
The warrior-lion, matchless in speed,
Seized that exceedingly venomous infidel
With a hero’s might,
Grabbing her by her black hair.
By the hearth stood a stone trivet;
Onto that stone trivet
He lifted and flung the woman.
The warrior upheld by the spirit Shay
Revealed himself a true lion;
When he struck the woman unerringly,
She split in two through the middle.
Its haft was steel, its point was sharp,
Black hardening ran along its edge,
Its blade gaped a handspan wide
And spread blood wherever it struck.
Laid upon grass, it set it aflame;
Those it struck died at once.
Its crown was like a mace’s fist,
And its haft was fashioned of steel;
When swung, its edge glowed red,
And no place it touched remained unharmed.
So that its victim would fester and rot,
So that death would overtake
All whom it touched without exception,
Bölökbay the master smith
Tempered it sixty times
In a dragon’s venom
And honed its edge keen.
Saying its blade was hard as crystal,
He polished it again and again;
The noble smith Bölökbay
Forged it together with Davut.
He snatched up and swung Aibalta,
The battle-axe left by great-hearted Manas,
And from the shrieking woman
He struck off the head.
Her heart aching, her insides boiling,
Distraught and burning with grief,
Tensed like a steed beneath a hero,
Her eyes dimmed and reddened,
Her whip-slim waist twisting,
To confront Kanchoro,
To stand as protector
For her brother-in-law, the gray-maned warrior,
And, if she found the chance,
